beats.narration_text: ChatGPT writes one word at a time, and every word comes out of a giant neural net. This is Sai. In twenty twenty-three, Stephen Wolfram opened nets like that one up, one picture at a time. This is part one: what the parts are, and where their numbers come from.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hello, Sai'
three plain result lines land
'two nets can fit and still disagree' lands last and holds

props.command: Stephen Wolfram wrote a long explainer on what ChatGPT is doing. Start with the neural net itself: what are its parts, where do their numbers come from, and can two trained nets disagree?
output: every part is simple: multiply, add, clip
the weights are learned, never written
two nets can fit and still disagree

beats.narration_text: Start with the parts. A neural net is layers of artificial neurons. Each one takes in numbers, weighs them, adds them up, and passes a single number on through a simple function. Write out everything this tiny net computes and you get one tangled formula. ChatGPT, Wolfram writes, is a formula like that, with billions of terms.

show.event: Wolfram's small net, weights on every neuron, is up first
the activation curves arrive with 'a simple function'
the written-out formula lands with 'one tangled formula'

panels.caption: A small net: every neuron weighs its inputs
The simple function each neuron applies
The whole tiny net, written out as one formula

plate.credit: Figures: Stephen Wolfram, “What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work?” (2023) · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

video.note: Stephen Wolfram's figures (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, sidecars in images/src/) composed on the reel's cream and revealed on the narration's cue. The portrait plate is RE-COMPOSED, never centre-cut.

beats.narration_text: Here's one neuron, the way Wolfram writes it. Multiply the inputs by weights, add a constant b, and apply a function f. In his examples, f is ray-loo: it turns any negative number into zero. Say the weights are one half and minus point eight, both inputs are one, and b is point one. The sum is minus point two, so the neuron outputs zero.

show.event: f(w·x + b) typesets
ReLU is defined as max(0, z) beneath it
the worked case evaluates to f(−0.2) = 0

props.title: One neuron, the way Wolfram writes it
props.note: Weigh the inputs, add a constant, turn negatives into zero.
props.conditions: w: weights · x: inputs · b: a constant · f: the activation (Wolfram's Ramp, i.e. ReLU). Example values are constructed: w = (0.5, −0.8), x = (1, 1), b = 0.1. GPT-2 itself uses GELU, a smooth cousin of ReLU.

beats.narration_text: Nobody types those weights in. Training shows the net examples, measures how far off its answers are, and nudges every weight downhill on that error, like water running down a mountain. It settles into some mountain lake, not always the lowest one. Even this toy net needed millions of examples to learn one simple shape. And train it twice, and you can get nets that agree on the examples but not beyond them.

show.event: the loss landscape with two descent paths is up first
the four training runs, 10k to 10M examples, fade in
four equally good nets disagree outside the shaded data

panels.caption: Downhill on the error: two starts, two different lakes
Four nets, same examples (white): different guesses beyond them

plate.credit: Figures: Stephen Wolfram, “What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work?” (2023) · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

video.note: Stephen Wolfram's figures (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, sidecars in images/src/) composed on the reel's cream and revealed on the narration's cue. The portrait plate is RE-COMPOSED, never centre-cut.

beats.narration_text: So which net is right? Wolfram's answer is blunt: there's really no way to say. Both are consistent with every example they were shown. Each just has its own built-in way of guessing beyond them, and some of those guesses look more reasonable to us than others. That's the black box in miniature: you can check the fit, not the reasoning.

show.event: the question splits into two nets that both fit
their guesses part ways past the data
the resolver: no way to say which is right

data.question: Both nets fit every training example. Which one is right?

resolver.label: There's no way to say
resolver.detail: both are consistent with the data; each has its own built-in way to guess beyond it

data.ghostText: you can check the fit, not the reasoning

beats.narration_text: We tried it on this Mac. Ten small nets, the same examples of a step shape, different random starts. All ten fit: the worst training error is point zero zero two two. Then ask each one about x equals three, outside the data. The answers run from minus point four three to two point eight four. Same data, same fit, no agreement.

show.event: ten nets, one task
the worst training error lands: every net fits
the lowest and highest guesses at x = 3 land, far apart

props.title: Ten nets, same examples, trained on this Mac
props.note: Constructed step task on [−1, 1], 400 points · 1-32-32-1 ReLU nets, seeds 0–9, Adam, 4,000 steps · evidence/train_nets.py, 26 Oct 2026

beats.narration_text: So, part one: every neuron does simple arithmetic, and nobody writes the weights. Training slides them downhill until the net fits its examples. But two nets can fit the same examples equally well and still disagree beyond them, and nothing in the fit tells you which guess to trust.

show.event: the one-page card opens
the learned-weights line fills in
'no way to say which is right' closes it

props.artifactHeading: How a net gets its numbers · one page
artifactLines: Every neuron does simple arithmetic: weigh the inputs, add a constant, apply a function such as ReLU.
Nobody writes the weights. Training slides them downhill on an error score until the examples fit.
Ten nets trained here fit the same examples (worst MSE 0.0022), yet guessed from -0.43 to 2.84 at x = 3.
Wolfram: there's really no way to say which is right. The fit is checkable; the reasoning isn't.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Ask an assistant for a short script that trains two tiny nets on the same points, with different random seeds. Run it, and plot both nets past the edge of your data. Then ask the hard question: where they disagree, which one would you trust, and how would you find out?

show.event: the handoff prompt types in under 'Your turn.'
the two seeds and the −3 to 3 plot are named
the last clause lands and the cursor holds
